## The problem {.smaller}

Most trading research runs on **bars** — minute, hourly, daily. That throws away
the mechanism by which price is actually formed.

At tick frequency the order book exposes the mechanism directly: queue
imbalance, depth, the sign of trade flow, the spread you must cross.

**Research question.** Can a reinforcement learning agent extract a tradable
signal from limit-order-book microstructure — and what bounds that signal
economically?

::: {.fragment}
Two design commitments follow:

- **Continuous exposure**, not discrete buy/hold/sell — position is a real number in $[-1, 1]$
- **Risk-adjusted reward** (Differential Sharpe Ratio), not raw P&L
:::

## Data {.smaller}

Real market-by-price data, not simulation.

| | |
|---|---|
| Source | DataBento MBP-10, Nasdaq |
| Instruments | AAPL, AMZN, AVGO, META, MSFT, TSLA |
| Training | 18,707,348 events, 25–27 Feb 2026 |
| Validation | 3,673,436 events, 2 Mar 2026 (first half) |
| Test | 3,673,439 events, 2 Mar 2026 (second half) |

: {tbl-colwidths="[25,75]"}

::: {.fragment}
Ten curated microstructure features: book imbalance, depth, flow, spread,
realised volatility, signed trade flow.

**Split is strictly temporal.** Scalers are fit on train only.
:::

## Method {.smaller}

**TD3** — Twin Delayed DDPG — chosen for continuous action control:

- Twin critics, taking the minimum, to damp overestimation bias
- Delayed policy updates (actor updated every second critic step)
- Target policy smoothing

Benchmarked against **DDPG**, **PPO**, a **random-action control**, and
**TWAP / VWAP / buy-and-hold**.

::: {.fragment}
**Reward: Differential Sharpe Ratio.** An online, recursive approximation to
the Sharpe ratio, so risk enters the objective at every step rather than being
scored after the fact.
:::

## H1 — Does the agent learn anything? {.smaller}

Frictionless mid-price execution, full held-out test window:

| Algorithm | Return | Sharpe | Max DD | Profit factor | Turnover |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **TD3** | 304.94% | 5.04 | −0.65% | 3.41 | 0.446 |
| DDPG | 312.78% | 4.96 | −0.45% | 3.64 | 0.401 |
| PPO | 205.55% | 5.44 | −0.47% | 4.59 | 0.363 |
| Random control | 0.25% | 0.03 | −0.59% | 1.01 | 0.667 |

::: {.fragment}
The **random control is the important row**. Same environment, same frictionless
assumption, 0.25% and Sharpe 0.03. The learned result is not an artifact of the
simulator.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The three learners are **close to each other**. TD3 does not dominate — DDPG
earns more, PPO has the better Sharpe. I do not claim TD3 is the right choice;
I claim all three learn.
:::

## The result that matters most {.smaller}

Those returns assume you trade at the **mid-price for free**. You cannot.

Re-pricing the identical action path at the bid/ask, charging the realised
turnover times each instrument's mean half-spread:

| Symbol | Gross PnL | Spread cost | Ratio | Net PnL |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| AAPL | 1.515 | 22.956 | 15.2× | **−21.44** |
| TSLA | 1.822 | 30.024 | 16.5× | **−28.20** |
| AMZN | 2.048 | 33.854 | 16.5× | **−31.81** |
| MSFT | 0.824 | 16.046 | 19.5× | **−15.22** |
| AVGO | 0.789 | 19.826 | 25.1× | **−19.04** |
| META | 0.288 | 10.836 | 37.6× | **−10.55** |

::: {.fragment}
**The edge does not survive the spread on any of the six.** The signal is real;
it is roughly an order of magnitude too small to pay for the trading it requires.
:::

## Why it dies: turnover, not signal quality {.smaller}

The mechanism is specific and measurable (AAPL):

- Position saturated at $\pm 1$ on **85%** of steps
- Turnover of **0.427** of position per step
- Gross earnings: **~1.6 × 10⁻⁶** per step
- Half-spread cost: **~2.4 × 10⁻⁵** per step

::: {.fragment}
The agent pays the spread roughly every other step to capture a fraction of a
tick. Break-even proportional fee is **0.037 bp** — far below any real venue.
:::

::: {.fragment}
This is not a failure of the agent. It is the agent optimising exactly what it
was given: a reward with **no cost term**. The mid-price assumption is in the
training objective, so re-scoring the checkpoint is not enough — a cost-aware
policy must be **retrained**, not rescored.
:::

## H2, H3, H4 {.smaller}

**H2 — cost sensitivity. Supported.** Independently trained policies stay active
at 0 and 0.01 bp, then collapse to static positions at higher fees. Cost
sensitivity is confirmed; a clean break-even point is not.

::: {.fragment}
**H3 — feature set. Unresolved.** Of three feature configurations, only the
curated ten-feature microstructure state converged. The other two did not train.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**H4 — reward objective. Unresolved.** Only the Differential Sharpe objective
produced a trading policy. The log-return objective did not train, so the
comparison turns on whether optimisation succeeded, not on what the objective
rewards.
:::

::: {.fragment}
I report H3 and H4 as **unresolved rather than negative**. A run that did not
train is not evidence about the quantity under study.
:::

## Contribution and limitations {.smaller}

**What this thesis contributes**

- A reproducible pipeline: raw MBP-10 → microstructure features → DSR reward → out-of-sample evaluation
- An economic bound on the tick-frequency edge, measured on all six instruments rather than asserted
- A negative result stated plainly, with the mechanism identified

::: {.fragment}
**What it does not establish**

- Four trading days, test confined to half a session — no regime or walk-forward evidence
- One seed per configuration; no distribution over random initialisations
- No non-RL baseline trained on the same features
- Zero latency assumed throughout
:::

## Conclusion {.smaller}

A TD3 agent trained on order-book microstructure learns a **genuine,
out-of-sample, risk-adjusted edge** at tick frequency — clearly separated from a
random control.

::: {.fragment}
That edge is **eliminated by the cost of crossing the spread** on every
instrument tested.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The honest reading: microstructure RL at this frequency is a
**transaction-cost problem before it is a learning problem**. The next
experiment is not a better agent — it is the same agent retrained against an
explicit bid/ask fill rule.
:::

. . .

::: {.centered-thanks}
**Thank you.**
:::

# Backup slides {.centered background-color="#1a1a2e"}

## Reviewer Q1 — Win + Lose sums across policies {.smaller}

> *At zero fee, why do the Win+Lose sums differ across policies?*

The printed figures reproduce exactly from the metrics
(win rate + lose rate): TWAP/VWAP 20.27%, TD3 31.87%, DDPG 41.08%, PPO 48.01%.

Win+Lose is the fraction of steps with a **non-zero position-weighted return**,
which requires both that the price moved **and** that the position was non-zero
at that step. Roughly 80–90% of consecutive LOB returns are zero, so the ceiling
is policy-independent — but the realised share is not, because position
magnitude varies across policies and the pooled figure averages six instruments
with different event frequencies.

::: {.fragment}
**Candid answer:** the arithmetic reconciliation from raw per-step returns to
these pooled shares is still open. I can state the mechanism but I would not
yet defend the exact decomposition.
:::

## Reviewer Q2 — 21,776 position changes vs 0.53 turnover {.smaller}

> *0.53 × 3,673,439 steps implies ~970,000 non-zero position changes, not 21,776.*

The reviewer is right that the two cannot both describe the same quantity.

- **Turnover** is the mean absolute position change per step, over *all* steps — a continuous quantity
- **21,776** counts something discrete and much rarer — evidently a thresholded or direction-reversing subset, not every non-zero change

::: {.fragment}
Both numbers appear in one sentence without their definitions, which makes them
read as contradictory. The correct fix is to print both definitions explicitly,
or drop the count. **This is a reporting defect in the thesis, and the reviewer
found it correctly.**
:::

## Reviewer Q3 — Extend repricing to all six {.smaller}

> *Can the bid/ask repricing be extended from one instrument to all six?*

**Yes — done, and it is on slide 5.**

The half-spread was already tabulated per instrument. The per-step edge came
from per-instrument test rollouts of the same TD3 checkpoint.

::: {.fragment}
The conclusion **strengthens** rather than weakens: the sign reversal is not an
AAPL artifact. Spread cost exceeds gross profit on all six, from 15.2× to 37.6×.

One caveat I want to state before being asked: this re-prices a **fixed action
path**. A policy trained against spread costs would not follow this path, so
this bounds *this* policy, not what a cost-aware agent could achieve.
:::

## Why TD3 rather than DQN {.smaller}

Exposure is naturally continuous. Discretising it into buy/hold/sell throws away
the sizing decision, which at tick frequency is most of the decision.

- **DQN** requires a discrete action space
- **DDPG** handles continuous actions but overestimates Q-values
- **TD3** adds twin critics, delayed actor updates and target smoothing to control exactly that bias

::: {.fragment}
Empirically DDPG and TD3 land close together here — consistent with the thesis's
own finding that **algorithm choice mattered less than state and reward
specification**.
:::

## Differential Sharpe Ratio {.smaller}

Sharpe is a property of a *distribution* of returns — it cannot be assigned to a
single step. The DSR resolves this with exponentially weighted moments:

$$A_t = A_{t-1} + \eta(R_t - A_{t-1}), \qquad B_t = B_{t-1} + \eta(R_t^2 - B_{t-1})$$

$$D_t = \frac{B_{t-1}\,\Delta A_t - \tfrac{1}{2}A_{t-1}\,\Delta B_t}{\left(B_{t-1} - A_{t-1}^2\right)^{3/2}}$$

$D_t$ is the first-order contribution of the current step to the running Sharpe
ratio, so risk enters the reward at every step rather than being scored
afterwards.

::: {.fragment}
It is also what produced the **only** trading policy among the reward objectives
tested (H4).
:::
